error_modes.label: Immediate action items and checklist discipline in the formation environment

texts.0: SP, due to unrehearsed recall of the memory items for the malfunction encountered, did not complete the immediate action items before moving to the checklist and reversed two critical steps of the sequence. The wrong item was worked while the abnormal indication remained unaddressed. IP intervened to stop the incorrect selection, took the aircraft and re-started the procedure from the beginning.
texts.1: SP, due to unrehearsed recall of the memory items, did not initiate the immediate action items on recognition of the malfunction and started only after two verbal prompts from IP, completing the sequence at the limit of the acceptable interval. The remaining checklist steps were performed in the correct order only after verbal direction on each item. No control input by IP was required, but every step depended on prompting.
texts.2: SP, due to an interrupted cockpit flow after the abnormal indication, did not start the immediate action items at the first opportunity and lost several seconds before the first selection. SP recognized the omission unaided, restated the indication and completed the remaining steps in the published order. Timing remained inside standards and no prompting or IP input was needed.
texts.3: SP identified the abnormal indication, called it to the Leader and completed the immediate action items in the published order without hesitation. Checklist steps were accomplished with correct switch identification, confirmed aloud before actuation. Aircraft control and formation position were maintained throughout the procedure.
texts.4: SP identified the abnormal indication at its onset, completed the immediate action items in the published order with no mis-selection and continued into the checklist without any break in the instrument scan. Every step was verified and confirmed aloud before actuation. Aircraft control, formation position and radio work were carried on simultaneously with no degradation of any of the three.
texts.marginal: SP completed the immediate action items within standards, but on both occasions in this sortie the first selection followed the indication only after a noticeable pause. The pattern indicates the memory items are being reconstructed rather than known cold. SP is expected to achieve immediate, unprompted initiation on the next sorties.

texts_at.1: SP completed the remaining checklist steps in the correct order, though the immediate action items were initiated only after two verbal prompts and every step depended on prompting, with the sequence completed at the limit of the acceptable interval. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training. SP is expected to initiate the immediate action items on recognition, before the verbal prompt on the next sortie.
texts_at.2: SP lost several seconds before the first selection after an interrupted cockpit flow following the abnormal indication delayed the start of the immediate action items, recognizing the omission unaided, restating the indication and completing the remaining steps in the published order, with timing inside standards and no prompting or IP input needed. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to protect the cockpit flow through the interruption so the first selection is not delayed.
texts_at.3: SP completed the immediate action items within standards, though on both occasions in this sortie the first selection followed the indication only after a noticeable pause, a pattern indicating the memory items are being reconstructed rather than known cold. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to achieve immediate, unprompted initiation on the next sorties.

texts_above.2: SP lost several seconds before the first selection after an interrupted cockpit flow following the abnormal indication delayed the start of the immediate action items, recognizing the omission unaided, restating the indication and completing the remaining steps in the published order, with no prompting from the IP and timing inside standards. Protecting the cockpit flow through the interruption would remove the delay entirely. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to good recovery of the immediate action sequence after an interrupted cockpit flow.
texts_above.3: SP identified the abnormal indication, called it to the Leader and completed the immediate action items in the published order without hesitation, with checklist steps accomplished through correct switch identification confirmed aloud before actuation and aircraft control and formation position maintained throughout the procedure. The only refinement left is to hold the same fluency on a second, unrelated malfunction later in the sortie. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to very good fluency in the immediate action sequence.
texts_above.4: SP identified the abnormal indication at its onset, completed the immediate action items in the published order with no mis-selection and continued into the checklist without any break in the instrument scan, with every step verified and confirmed aloud before actuation and aircraft control, formation position and radio work carried on simultaneously with no degradation of any of the three. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to excellent integration of the checklist flow with aircraft control and radio work.

error_modes.label: Lost wingman procedure flown from the Wingman position (VMC and IMC)

texts.0: SP, due to an unrehearsed lost wingman procedure, did not execute the briefed turn away from the Leader on losing visual contact and remained on the formation heading while the aircraft drifted toward the Leader's flight path. Separation was never established by SP and the divergence had to be commanded and then flown by IP. The subsequent altitude change and heading were performed entirely under IP direction.
texts.1: SP, due to hesitation in accepting that visual contact was actually lost, did not initiate the lost wingman turn on recognition and began the divergence only after direction, at the latest acceptable point. Turn direction, bank and altitude change were then flown correctly, but each element required a separate verbal cue. Separation was achieved without control input by IP.
texts.2: SP, due to a delayed decision on the loss of visual contact, did not begin the divergence at the first opportunity and held the formation heading for a few seconds longer than briefed. SP then recognized the situation unaided, turned away from the Leader and established the briefed altitude change without prompting. Separation was built up well inside the standards and the procedure was flown to completion.
texts.3: SP recognized the loss of visual contact without delay, announced it and flew the briefed lost wingman turn away from the Leader with correct bank and timing. The associated altitude change was made as briefed and the divergence heading was held for the full required interval. Transition to instruments was made without any attitude excursion.
texts.4: SP announced the loss of visual contact at the moment it occurred and flew the lost wingman procedure with turn direction, bank, timing and altitude change matching the briefed values exactly. The instrument transition produced no attitude or airspeed excursion and the divergence heading was held for the full interval without deviation. SP kept the Leader informed throughout and had the subsequent recovery plan ready before being asked for it.
texts.marginal: SP flew the lost wingman procedure within standards, but the turn away was started at the late end of the acceptable window on both repetitions and the bank was consistently shallower than briefed. The trend shows the decision to accept loss of visual contact is being deferred. SP is expected to commit to the procedure at the first indication on subsequent sorties.

texts_at.1: SP flew the turn direction, bank and altitude change correctly once the divergence had begun, though the divergence started only after direction at the latest acceptable point and each element required a separate verbal cue, with separation achieved without control input by IP. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training. SP is expected to initiate the divergence on recognition, before the verbal prompt on the next sortie.
texts_at.2: SP held the formation heading a few seconds longer than briefed after a delayed decision on the loss of visual contact, then recognizing the situation unaided, turning away from the Leader and establishing the briefed altitude change without prompting, with separation built up well inside the standards and the procedure flown to completion. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to accept the loss of visual contact at the first opportunity so the heading is not held past it.
texts_at.3: SP flew the lost wingman procedure within standards, though the turn away was started at the late end of the acceptable window on both repetitions and the bank was consistently shallower than briefed, showing the decision to accept loss of visual contact is being deferred. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to commit to the procedure at the first indication on subsequent sorties.

texts_above.2: SP held the formation heading a few seconds longer than briefed after a delayed decision on the loss of visual contact, then recognizing the situation unaided, turning away from the Leader and establishing the briefed altitude change without prompting, with no prompting from the IP and separation built up well inside the standards. Accepting the loss of visual contact at the first opportunity would remove the extra seconds entirely. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to sound recovery of the divergence decision within the acceptable window.
texts_above.3: SP recognized the loss of visual contact without delay, announced it and flew the briefed lost wingman turn away from the Leader with correct bank and timing, with the associated altitude change made as briefed and the divergence heading held for the full required interval, and the transition to instruments producing no attitude excursion. The only refinement left is to hold the same commitment on a second, closely following loss of sight. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to sure-handed commitment to the procedure at the first indication.
texts_above.4: SP announced the loss of visual contact at the moment it occurred and flew the lost wingman procedure with turn direction, bank, timing and altitude change matching the briefed values exactly, with the instrument transition producing no attitude or airspeed excursion, the divergence heading held for the full interval without deviation, and the Leader kept informed throughout with the subsequent recovery plan ready before being asked for it. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exceptional precision in matching every briefed value of the divergence.

error_modes.label: Lost wingman deconfliction and predictable flight path as Leader

texts.0: SP, as Leader, due to an incomplete picture of the wingman's last known position, did not maintain the briefed heading, altitude and airspeed after the lost wingman call and started a turn toward the side the wingman was diverging to. The predictable flight path required for deconfliction was not provided and lateral separation was not assured. IP intervened, took the aircraft and restored the briefed parameters.
texts.1: SP, as Leader, due to task saturation after the lost wingman call, did not hold the briefed parameters and allowed heading and airspeed to wander until directed to freeze them, recovering the required flight path at the limit of the acceptable interval. Deconfliction was preserved only because IP prompted the parameter to be held on each occasion. No control input by IP was required.
texts.2: SP, as Leader, due to attention shifting to the radio call, did not hold the briefed airspeed immediately after the lost wingman call and allowed it to drift from the formation value. SP detected the drift unaided, restored the briefed heading, altitude and airspeed and stated them to the wingman. Deconfliction was never in question and no prompting was needed.
texts.3: SP, as Leader, acknowledged the lost wingman call at once and held the briefed heading, altitude and airspeed to provide a predictable flight path for the deconfliction. The wingman was given the parameters being flown and the intentions for the recovery. Separation responsibilities were discharged without any prompting.
texts.4: SP, as Leader, acknowledged the lost wingman call immediately, froze the briefed heading, altitude and airspeed with no measurable drift and stated them to the wingman in one concise transmission. Intentions for the subsequent recovery and rejoin were passed before they were requested. The deconfliction was managed while the SP continued to fly the profile and to work the radios without degradation.
texts.marginal: SP held the briefed parameters after the lost wingman call within standards, but airspeed was allowed to creep on each repetition before being restored. The trend indicates that the priority of a frozen flight path is not yet automatic when the radio workload rises. SP is expected to hold the deconfliction parameters without drift on the next sorties.

texts_at.1: SP, as Leader, recovered the required flight path, though the recovery followed only once IP prompted the parameter to be held on each occasion, with deconfliction preserved only through IP direction and no control input by IP required. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training. SP is expected to hold the briefed parameters on the own initiative before the verbal prompt on the next sortie.
texts_at.2: SP, as Leader, allowed the briefed airspeed to drift from the formation value after attention shifted to the radio call, detecting the drift unaided, restoring the briefed heading, altitude and airspeed and stating them to the wingman, with deconfliction never in question and no prompting needed. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to hold the briefed airspeed through the radio call so the drift does not occur.
texts_at.3: SP, as Leader, held the briefed parameters after the lost wingman call within standards, though airspeed was allowed to creep on each repetition before being restored, showing that the priority of a frozen flight path is not yet automatic when the radio workload rises. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to hold the deconfliction parameters without drift on the next sorties.

texts_above.2: SP, as Leader, allowed the briefed airspeed to drift from the formation value after attention shifted to the radio call, detecting the drift unaided, restoring the briefed heading, altitude and airspeed and stating them to the wingman, with no prompting from the IP and deconfliction never in question. Holding the briefed airspeed through the radio call would remove the drift entirely. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to solid recovery of the briefed airspeed once the radio call was complete.
texts_above.3: SP, as Leader, acknowledged the lost wingman call at once and held the briefed heading, altitude and airspeed to provide a predictable flight path for the deconfliction, with the wingman given the parameters being flown and the intentions for the recovery, and separation responsibilities discharged without any prompting. The only refinement left is to hold the same frozen flight path through a second radio call arriving close behind the first. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to well-developed discipline in holding a predictable flight path.
texts_above.4: SP, as Leader, acknowledged the lost wingman call immediately, froze the briefed heading, altitude and airspeed with no measurable drift and stated them to the wingman in one concise transmission, with intentions for the subsequent recovery and rejoin passed before they were requested and the deconfliction managed while SP continued to fly the profile and to work the radios without degradation. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to outstanding steadiness of the frozen flight path through the radio workload.

error_modes.label: Timely notification of the Leader and transition to IFR flight from the Wingman position

texts.0: SP, due to lack of assertiveness in voicing a recognized unsafe condition, did not inform the Leader that the formation position could no longer be safely maintained and stayed in position after the visual references were lost. The transition to IFR flight was not initiated and the aircraft was flown on outside references that were no longer usable. IP took the aircraft to establish separation and instrument flight.
texts.1: SP, due to lack of assertiveness in stating an inability to comply, did not inform the Leader at the point the condition was recognized and transmitted only after being prompted twice, at the limit of the acceptable interval. The transition to instrument flight followed the call correctly but was initiated on IP direction. No control input by IP was required.
texts.2: SP, due to reluctance to interrupt the Leader on the radio, did not pass the required information at the first opportunity and delayed the call by a few seconds. SP then made the transmission unaided, stated the condition clearly and completed the transition to instrument flight without further delay. The delay stayed inside the standards and no prompting was needed.
texts.3: SP informed the Leader as soon as the condition was recognized, using a clear and complete statement of the problem and the intention. The transition to IFR flight was made promptly, with the instrument scan established before the outside references were lost. Aircraft control and separation from the Leader were maintained throughout.
texts.4: SP informed the Leader at the instant the condition was recognized, in one unambiguous transmission that carried both the problem and the intended action. The transition to IFR flight was made with the instrument scan already established and produced no attitude, heading or airspeed excursion. SP then confirmed the plan with the Leader and had the alternative course of action ready if the first was refused.
texts.marginal: SP informed the Leader and transitioned to instrument flight within standards, but each transmission was made after a visible pause and was phrased as a question rather than a statement. The trend shows a reluctance to assert a recognized condition upward. SP is expected to make the call at the moment of recognition, in a direct form, on subsequent sorties.

texts_at.1: SP made the transmission and completed the transition to instrument flight, though the transmission followed only once IP prompted twice, with the transition initiated on IP direction and no control input by IP required. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training. SP is expected to inform the Leader at the point the condition is recognized, before the verbal prompt on the next sortie.
texts_at.2: SP delayed the call by a few seconds after reluctance to interrupt the Leader on the radio, then making the transmission unaided, stating the condition clearly and completing the transition to instrument flight without further delay, with the delay staying inside the standards and no prompting needed. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to interrupt the Leader's exchange at the point the condition is recognized so the delay is not needed.
texts_at.3: SP informed the Leader and transitioned to instrument flight within standards, though each transmission was made after a visible pause and was phrased as a question rather than a statement, showing a reluctance to assert a recognized condition upward. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to make the call at the moment of recognition, in a direct form, on subsequent sorties.

texts_above.2: SP delayed the call by a few seconds after reluctance to interrupt the Leader on the radio, then making the transmission unaided, stating the condition clearly and completing the transition to instrument flight without further delay, with no prompting from the IP and the delay staying inside the standards. Interrupting the Leader's exchange at the point of recognition would remove the delay entirely. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to steady recovery of the notification once the delay was recognized.
texts_above.3: SP informed the Leader as soon as the condition was recognized, using a clear and complete statement of the problem and the intention, with the transition to IFR flight made promptly and the instrument scan established before the outside references were lost, and aircraft control and separation from the Leader maintained throughout. The only refinement left is to hold the same directness under a busier radio load. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to consistently accurate directness in every notification to the Leader.
texts_above.4: SP informed the Leader at the instant the condition was recognized, in one unambiguous transmission that carried both the problem and the intended action, with the transition to IFR flight made with the instrument scan already established and producing no attitude, heading or airspeed excursion, and the plan then confirmed with the Leader with an alternative course of action ready if the first was refused. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exemplary directness that left the Leader in no doubt of the problem or the intended action.

error_modes.label: Notification of ATC and obtaining IFR clearance in an actual situation

texts.0: SP, due to a technically worded transmission where plain language was required to convey the emergency, did not inform ATC of the actual condition and did not request the IFR clearance. The controller was left without the aircraft's status, position or intentions, and no clearance was obtained before entering controlled airspace in instrument conditions. IP took the radios and made the declaration.
texts.1: SP, due to jargon that obscured the aircraft's actual condition, did not state the emergency in terms the controller could act upon and reworded the transmission only after two prompts, obtaining the IFR clearance at the limit of the acceptable interval. Aircraft type, position, condition and intentions were passed only when each item was requested. No control input by IP was required.
texts.2: SP, due to an initial transmission that omitted the intentions, did not give ATC the complete picture at the first call and had to amplify it in a second transmission. SP recognized the omission unaided, restated the condition in plain language and obtained the IFR clearance without further delay. The exchange stayed inside the standards and no prompting was required.
texts.3: SP informed ATC promptly, stated the nature of the emergency in plain language with position, intentions and persons on board, and obtained the IFR clearance before it was needed. The read-back confirmed the actual clearance issued. Aircraft control and formation deconfliction were maintained while the radio work was carried out.
texts.4: SP informed ATC at the first opportunity with a single complete transmission covering the nature of the emergency, position, intentions, fuel and persons on board in plain language. The IFR clearance was obtained and read back accurately well before the aircraft required it, and the subsequent amendment was accepted without hesitation. Radio workload was absorbed with no effect on aircraft control or on the formation deconfliction.
texts.marginal: SP notified ATC and obtained the IFR clearance within standards, but the first transmission on each occasion omitted the intentions and had to be amplified. The trend indicates the report format is not yet consolidated under the radio workload of an actual situation. SP is expected to pass a complete first call on subsequent sorties.

texts_at.1: SP obtained the IFR clearance, though the reworded transmission followed only once IP prompted it twice, with aircraft type, position, condition and intentions passed only when each item was requested and no control input by IP required. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training. SP is expected to state the emergency in plain language on the first transmission, before the verbal prompt on the next sortie.
texts_at.2: SP omitted the intentions from the first transmission and had to amplify it in a second transmission, recognizing the omission unaided, restating the condition in plain language and obtaining the IFR clearance without further delay, with the exchange staying inside the standards and no prompting required. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to include the intentions in the first transmission so the amplification is not needed.
texts_at.3: SP notified ATC and obtained the IFR clearance within standards, though the first transmission on each occasion omitted the intentions and had to be amplified, showing the report format is not yet consolidated under the radio workload of an actual situation. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to pass a complete first call on subsequent sorties.

texts_above.2: SP omitted the intentions from the first transmission and had to amplify it in a second transmission, recognizing the omission unaided, restating the condition in plain language and obtaining the IFR clearance without further delay, with no prompting from the IP and the exchange staying inside the standards. Including the intentions in the first transmission would remove the amplification entirely. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to dependable recovery of the complete picture on the second transmission.
texts_above.3: SP informed ATC promptly, stated the nature of the emergency in plain language with position, intentions and persons on board, and obtained the IFR clearance before it was needed, with the read-back confirming the actual clearance issued and aircraft control and formation deconfliction maintained while the radio work was carried out. The only refinement left is to hold the same completeness on the first call under a heavier radio load. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to notably good completeness in the first ATC transmission.
texts_above.4: SP informed ATC at the first opportunity with a single complete transmission covering the nature of the emergency, position, intentions, fuel and persons on board in plain language, with the IFR clearance obtained and read back accurately well before the aircraft required it, the subsequent amendment accepted without hesitation, and the radio workload absorbed with no effect on aircraft control or on the formation deconfliction. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to superior completeness sustained through the first transmission and the subsequent amendment.

error_modes.label: Assistance to the formation member suffering the emergency

texts.0: SP, due to an unassigned division of responsibilities within the formation, did not provide assistance to the member declaring the emergency and neither took nor offered the lead for the recovery. No visual assessment of the affected aircraft was carried out and the required calls were left unmade. IP intervened, directed the assistance and assigned the roles.
texts.1: SP, due to an unassigned division of responsibilities, did not offer assistance on the declaration and acted only after being told, taking up the escort position at the limit of the acceptable interval. The visual assessment of the affected aircraft and the calls to the emergency aircraft were made item by item on direction. No control input by IP was required.
texts.2: SP, due to attention held by the SP's own cockpit checks, did not begin the assessment of the affected aircraft at the first opportunity and delayed taking up the escort position. SP then recognized the requirement unaided, moved to a safe observation position and passed the assessment to the affected aircraft. The delay stayed inside the standards and no prompting was needed.
texts.3: SP acknowledged the emergency declaration at once, took up a safe observation position and passed a complete external assessment of the affected aircraft. The recovery was organized with a clear division of responsibilities and the affected aircraft was kept informed. Safe separation from the affected aircraft was maintained throughout.
texts.4: SP acknowledged the declaration immediately, moved to a safe observation position with correct closure and passed a complete and accurate external assessment without being asked. The recovery was organized with roles stated aloud, the affected aircraft was relieved of the navigation and radio workload, and the plan was updated as the condition changed. Separation, position and radio work were managed simultaneously with no degradation.
texts.marginal: SP provided the required assistance within standards, but the external assessment was passed only after the affected aircraft asked for it on both occasions. The trend shows the escort role is being executed reactively rather than taken up on the declaration. SP is expected to initiate the assessment unprompted on subsequent sorties.

texts_at.1: SP took up the escort position and passed the visual assessment and the calls to the emergency aircraft, though each item followed only once directed, with the escort position taken up at the limit of the acceptable interval and no control input by IP required. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training. SP is expected to offer assistance on the declaration before the verbal prompt on the next sortie.
texts_at.2: SP delayed taking up the escort position after attention was held by the own cockpit checks and did not begin the assessment at the first opportunity, recognizing the requirement unaided, moving to a safe observation position and passing the assessment to the affected aircraft, with the delay staying inside the standards and no prompting needed. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to move to the escort position as soon as the declaration is heard so the delay does not occur.
texts_at.3: SP provided the required assistance within standards, though the external assessment was passed only after the affected aircraft asked for it on both occasions, showing the escort role is being executed reactively rather than taken up on the declaration. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to initiate the assessment unprompted on subsequent sorties.

texts_above.2: SP delayed taking up the escort position after attention was held by the own cockpit checks and did not begin the assessment at the first opportunity, recognizing the requirement unaided, moving to a safe observation position and passing the assessment to the affected aircraft, with no prompting from the IP and the delay staying inside the standards. Moving to the escort position as soon as the declaration is heard would remove the delay entirely. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to assured recovery of the escort role once the declaration was recognized.
texts_above.3: SP acknowledged the emergency declaration at once, took up a safe observation position and passed a complete external assessment of the affected aircraft, with the recovery organized with a clear division of responsibilities, the affected aircraft kept informed, and safe separation maintained throughout. The only refinement left is to hold the same promptness when the declaration arrives during a busier phase. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to precise organization of the recovery around the affected aircraft.
texts_above.4: SP acknowledged the declaration immediately, moved to a safe observation position with correct closure and passed a complete and accurate external assessment without being asked, with the recovery organized with roles stated aloud, the affected aircraft relieved of the navigation and radio workload, and the plan updated as the condition changed, and separation, position and radio work managed simultaneously with no degradation. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to first-rate organization that relieved the affected aircraft of every non-essential task.

error_modes.label: Contacting ground stations for an emergency aircraft that has lost R/T

texts.0: SP, due to no plan for the loss of the emergency aircraft's R/T, did not contact the ground stations on behalf of the affected aircraft and made no attempt to establish an alternative means of communication. The controlling agency was left without the emergency aircraft's status and intentions for the whole recovery. IP took the radios and passed the required information.
texts.1: SP, due to no plan for the loss of R/T, did not assume the relay function on recognition and started transmitting for the affected aircraft only after being directed, at the limit of the acceptable interval. Each element of the relay was passed on prompting rather than as a complete report. No control input by IP was required.
texts.2: SP, due to time spent on repeated attempts on the primary frequency, did not begin the relay at the first opportunity and delayed the first transmission to the ground station. SP then recognized the requirement unaided, established contact and relayed the affected aircraft's condition and intentions. The delay stayed inside the standards and no prompting was needed.
texts.3: SP recognized the loss of the emergency aircraft's R/T, assumed the relay function without delay and contacted the ground station with the affected aircraft's identification, condition and intentions. Visual signals were used to confirm the information with the affected aircraft before it was passed. The relay was maintained accurately for the remainder of the recovery.
texts.4: SP recognized the R/T failure at once, assumed the relay function without being asked and contacted the ground station with a complete, accurate report of the affected aircraft's identification, condition, position and intentions. Every subsequent instruction was relayed and confirmed with the affected aircraft by visual signals with no loss of content. The relay was carried on together with the escort position and the SP's own cockpit workload without degrading either.
texts.marginal: SP performed the radio relay within standards, but the reports omitted the affected aircraft's intentions until the ground station requested them. The trend indicates the relay format is not yet consolidated. SP is expected to pass complete, unprompted relay reports on subsequent sorties.

texts_at.1: SP passed each element of the relay once directed, though each item followed on prompting rather than as a complete report, with the relay function assumed only after direction and no control input by IP required. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training. SP is expected to assume the relay function on recognition, before the verbal prompt on the next sortie.
texts_at.2: SP delayed the first transmission after time was spent on repeated attempts on the primary frequency and the relay was not begun at the first opportunity, recognizing the requirement unaided, establishing contact and relaying the affected aircraft's condition and intentions, with the delay staying inside the standards and no prompting needed. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to move to the ground station frequency after the first unanswered attempt so the relay is not delayed.
texts_at.3: SP performed the radio relay within standards, though the reports omitted the affected aircraft's intentions until the ground station requested them, showing the relay format is not yet consolidated. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to pass complete, unprompted relay reports on subsequent sorties.

texts_above.2: SP delayed the first transmission after time was spent on repeated attempts on the primary frequency and the relay was not begun at the first opportunity, recognizing the requirement unaided, establishing contact and relaying the affected aircraft's condition and intentions, with no prompting from the IP and the delay staying inside the standards. Moving to the ground station frequency after the first unanswered attempt would remove the delay entirely. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to competent recovery of the relay once the primary frequency was abandoned.
texts_above.3: SP recognized the loss of the emergency aircraft's R/T, assumed the relay function without delay and contacted the ground station with the affected aircraft's identification, condition and intentions, with visual signals used to confirm the information with the affected aircraft before it was passed and the relay maintained accurately for the remainder of the recovery. The only refinement left is to hold the same completeness through a second ground station handoff. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to disciplined completeness in every relay report passed.
texts_above.4: SP recognized the R/T failure at once, assumed the relay function without being asked and contacted the ground station with a complete, accurate report of the affected aircraft's identification, condition, position and intentions, with every subsequent instruction relayed and confirmed with the affected aircraft by visual signals with no loss of content, and the relay carried on together with the escort position and the own cockpit workload without degrading either. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to faultless integration of the relay function with the escort role.

error_modes.label: Aircraft control and formation deconfliction while working the emergency

texts.0: SP, due to an attention bottleneck on a single caution indication at the expense of the instrument cross-check, did not continue to fly the aircraft while working the procedure and allowed altitude and heading to depart the briefed values without recognition. Separation from the other formation member was reduced without being noticed. IP intervened with control inputs to restore the flight path and the separation.
texts.1: SP, due to absorption in the cockpit indication, did not maintain the instrument cross-check during the procedure and allowed altitude and airspeed to reach the limit of the acceptable band before correcting. The deviation was reversed only after IP called each parameter aloud. No control input by IP was required, but the recovery depended entirely on the prompting.
texts.2: SP, due to attention held briefly by the caution indication, did not maintain the full instrument cross-check while running the checklist and allowed a small altitude and heading deviation to develop. SP detected the deviation unaided, returned to the briefed values and completed the procedure with the scan re-established. Separation from the other formation member was never in question and no prompting was needed.
texts.3: SP kept flying the aircraft as the first priority while working the emergency, holding the briefed altitude, heading and airspeed throughout the procedure. The instrument cross-check was maintained between checklist steps and the separation from the other formation member was continuously assessed. The procedure was completed without any parameter leaving the standards.

error_modes.label: Knowledge of the applicable emergency procedures in briefing and in flight

texts.1: SP, due to incomplete knowledge of the limits applicable to the procedure, did not state the required steps in the correct order and produced them at the limit of the acceptable interval only after successive cues. The applicable limitations were recalled only when each was named. The knowledge was sufficient to continue, but every item required prompting.
texts.2: SP, due to reliance on the checklist rather than on consolidated recall, did not state two steps of the procedure without a pause during the briefing. SP corrected the omission unaided within the same discussion and applied the procedure correctly and in the published order when it was presented in flight. No prompting was needed and the knowledge remained inside the standards.
texts.3: SP stated the applicable emergency procedures accurately in the briefing, including the boldface content, the associated limitations and the formation-specific requirements. texts.4: SP stated the applicable emergency procedures accurately and completely in the briefing, including boldface content, limitations, formation-specific requirements and the conditions that distinguish similar malfunctions. error_modes.label: Smoothness of control inputs during the lost wingman turn away

texts.0: SP, due to an abrupt roll into the lost wingman turn away instead of the smooth application of control inputs the procedure requires, did not contain the divergence to 15 degrees of bank and induced a pitch and bank excursion while transitioning to instruments. The 15 second interval was never timed and the aircraft was left in an attitude SP could not resolve against the instruments. IP took the aircraft, re-established wings level and flew the required separation.
texts.1: SP, due to abrupt control inputs on entering the lost wingman turn away, did not hold the procedure bank and rolled through roughly twice the required 15 degrees before the attitude was stabilized. The bank was corrected and the 15 second interval restarted only after IP called the attitude and then the recovery. The turn away finished at the limit of what could be accepted, with every correction driven by verbal direction.
texts.2: SP, due to a rapid initial roll input at the loss of visual contact, briefly passed 15 degrees of bank and introduced a small pitch excursion during the transition to instruments. SP recognized the excursion on the attitude indicator, smoothed the inputs and held the remaining seconds of the interval at the correct bank without prompting. Separation was established inside the required time.
texts.3: SP applied smooth control inputs on losing visual contact and established 15 degrees of bank away from the Leader, holding it for the full 15 seconds while transitioning to instruments. No attitude excursion was induced and the disorientation cues were not aggravated. Course was resumed and the separate clearance requested as briefed.
texts.4: SP flew the lost wingman turn away so smoothly that the attitude indicator showed one continuous roll to 15 degrees and back, with the interval timed exactly. The instrument transition produced no perceptible pitch or heading excursion and disorientation cues never developed. Deviations from the procedure bank and timing were negligible.
texts.marginal: SP kept the lost wingman turn away within standards, but both the roll in and the roll out were made with quicker inputs than the smooth application the procedure calls for, and a small pitch excursion accompanied each one. error_modes.label: Directed practice lost wingman started on acknowledgement instead of when ready

texts.0: SP, treating the acknowledgement of the Leader's practice lost wingman direction as the execution cue, began the procedure in the same moment, without being ready and without the associated radio call. The Leader was still maneuvering and received no warning of the divergence, so the deconfliction the exercise depends on was never set up. IP took the aircraft and terminated the exercise.
texts.1: SP, due to the same confusion between acknowledging the direction and executing it, started the divergence before the flight path was assessed and made the lost wingman call only after IP directed it. Separation remained acceptable but at the limit of what the exercise allows, and each remaining step was flown on verbal direction. No control input by IP was required.
texts.2: SP acknowledged the direction and started to roll away before being ready, then recognized within a second or two that neither the flight path assessment nor the radio call had been made. SP stopped the divergence, returned to the fingertip position, made the call and re-flew the procedure at the own initiative. The exercise was completed in VMC with separation never in question.
texts.3: SP acknowledged the Leader's direction with the call sign only and did not begin execution, then flew the appropriate lost wingman procedure when ready and made the associated radio call. The Leader was able to monitor the divergence throughout and SP ended the exercise with the visual call before a rejoin was directed.
texts.4: SP kept the acknowledgement and the execution clearly separate, confirmed flight path and instrument scan first, then flew the procedure and made the call as one uninterrupted sequence. The reference heading passed by the Leader was taken up before the visual call. Departures from the directed exercise sequence were negligible.

error_modes.label: Breakout initiation against the mandatory hazard, in front, told and lost SA criteria

texts.0: SP, having lost situational awareness and drifted in front of the Leader, did not initiate the breakout although the mandatory criteria were met, and attempted instead to recover the fingertip references from an unpredictable position. No clearing in the direction of the break was carried out and neither power nor speed brake was used, so separation continued to reduce. IP took the aircraft, cleared and flew the breakout.
texts.1: SP, due to the mandatory breakout criteria not being applied as they occurred, remained in an unsafe position until told twice to break out. The maneuver away from the Leader's last known position was begun at the limit of what still ensured separation and the breaking out call was made only after further prompting. No control input by IP was required.
texts.2: SP, due to hesitation over whether the criteria were met, left the position a few seconds late, then cleared in the direction of the break and maneuvered away from the Leader's last known position on the own initiative, using power and speed brake to expedite separation. The breaking out call was made as soon as able and safe separation was held until the Leader acknowledged.
texts.3: SP recognized that a mandatory breakout criterion was met, cleared in the direction of the break without delay and maneuvered away from the Leader's last known position, using power and speed brake as required to hold a safe maneuvering airspeed. The breaking out call was made as soon as able, the disorientation of passing clear of the Leader was anticipated, and SP did not rejoin until directed.
texts.4: SP applied the mandatory breakout criteria the moment the condition arose and flew the breakout as a controlled maneuver rather than the abrupt high G turn that is often assumed, clearing first and using power and speed brake to expedite the separation. Safe separation was maintained until the Leader confirmed visual contact, and the rejoin was flown only when directed. Deviations from the published breakout technique were negligible.

error_modes.label: Knock-It-Off discipline when the malfunction occurs during maneuvering

texts.0: SP, on encountering the malfunction while maneuvering, did not call Knock-It-Off and did not cease maneuvering, but worked the indication while the maneuver continued. The flight path was never cleared, the other member was left without the reason for the loss of position, and maneuvering was resumed without any verbal clearance. IP made the Knock-It-Off call and took the aircraft.
texts.1: SP, due to Knock-It-Off being treated as a call of last resort rather than the response to safety of flight doubt, continued the maneuver with the abnormal indication displayed and made the call only after two prompts. texts.2: SP, due to a few seconds spent diagnosing the indication before speaking, delayed the Knock-It-Off call, then made it unprompted, ceased maneuvering and cleared the flight path. texts.3: SP called Knock-It-Off as soon as the malfunction raised a safety of flight concern, cleared the flight path, ceased maneuvering and acknowledged in order of position in the formation. As Leader, SP continued the current maneuver without changing power setting so that the flight path stayed predictable for deconfliction, and no maneuvering was resumed before verbal clearance was obtained.
texts.4: SP made the Knock-It-Off call the moment doubt existed, with the flight path cleared and maneuvering stopped in one deliberate action, and held the power setting unchanged so that the other member could deconflict against a predictable flight path. The formation was reorganized and verbal clearance obtained before anything was resumed. Departures from the published Knock-It-Off sequence were negligible.
texts.marginal: SP applied the Knock-It-Off procedure within standards, but the call consistently followed the diagnosis instead of preceding it, and the power setting was adjusted slightly as the maneuvering stopped. The attitude was flown on sensation rather than on the instruments and the divergence was neither timed nor controlled. IP took the aircraft and recovered it to straight and level.
texts.1: SP, due to the onset of disorientation not being voiced, held the position with degraded control until IP required the condition to be declared. Control was then transferred and the attitude, altitude, heading and airspeed calls were accepted, but every step of the recovery was initiated by verbal direction at the limit of the acceptable delay.
texts.2: SP, due to a delayed recognition of the disorientation, remained in position for several seconds with an unreliable attitude picture, then informed the other aircraft unaided and asked for the attitude, altitude, heading and airspeed to be passed. The symptoms cleared during the straight and level period and the position was regained without any IP input.
texts.3: SP informed the other aircraft immediately on recognizing the disorientation and transferred aircraft control to the other pilot as it was practical to do so. In the Leader role, SP passed attitude, altitude, heading and airspeed to the wingman, established straight and level flight for 30 to 60 seconds and worked the formation toward visual conditions. A lost wingman procedure was correctly avoided while the symptoms persisted.
texts.4: SP declared the disorientation at the first symptom, arranged the transfer of control without hesitation and used the other crewmember to confirm the attitude before any input was made. As Leader, the straight and level relief period was flown for the full 30 to 60 seconds with continuous attitude, altitude, heading and airspeed calls, and the formation was taken to visual conditions. Deviations from the published disorientation procedure were negligible.
texts.marginal: SP managed the disorientation within standards, but the condition was declared only after it had persisted for several seconds and the offer to transfer control came from the other cockpit. The attitude advisories and the straight and level relief period were then used correctly. SP is expected to declare at the first symptom, since the value of the transfer and of the attitude calls falls away once the symptoms are established.

texts_at.1: SP accepted the transfer of control and the attitude, altitude, heading and airspeed calls, though every step was initiated by verbal direction at the limit of the acceptable delay, with the onset of disorientation not voiced until IP required the condition to be declared. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training. SP is expected to voice the onset of disorientation before the verbal prompt on the next sortie.
texts_at.2: SP remained in position for several seconds with an unreliable attitude picture after a delayed recognition of the disorientation, then informing the other aircraft unaided and asking for the attitude, altitude, heading and airspeed to be passed, with the symptoms clearing during the straight and level period and the position regained without any IP input. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to recognize the disorientation sooner so the unreliable attitude picture is not held for several seconds.
texts_at.3: SP managed the disorientation within standards, though the condition was declared only after it had persisted for several seconds and the offer to transfer control came from the other cockpit, with the attitude advisories and the straight and level relief period then used correctly. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to declare at the first symptom, since the value of the transfer and of the attitude calls falls away once the symptoms are established.

Recognizing the disorientation sooner would remove the unreliable attitude picture entirely. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to good recovery of the attitude picture once the disorientation was recognized.
texts_above.3: SP informed the other aircraft immediately on recognizing the disorientation and transferred aircraft control to the other pilot as it was practical to do so, and in the Leader role, passed attitude, altitude, heading and airspeed to the wingman, established straight and level flight for 30 to 60 seconds and worked the formation toward visual conditions, with a lost wingman procedure correctly avoided while the symptoms persisted. The only refinement left is to hold the same immediacy on a second onset later in the sortie. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to very good immediacy in declaring the disorientation to the other cockpit.

This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to excellent immediacy that declared the disorientation at the very first symptom.

error_modes.label: Sympathetic abort and runway side discipline during the formation takeoff
error_modes.source: technique:9.42 FORMATION TAKEOFF ABNORMALITIES AND ABORTS

texts.0: SP, startled by the other aircraft's abort call after brake release, aborted a serviceable aircraft although no element abort had been directed and no problem existed with the own aircraft. The respective side of the runway was not maintained during the deceleration and the two aircraft were brought into the same high speed abort with reducing lateral separation. IP took the aircraft to stop the departure from the assigned side.
texts.1: SP, due to the abort call being taken as an element abort without the operative word for the flight, initiated the abort and had to be told to continue, so power was restored late in the available runway. The respective side of the runway was held only after direction and the radio call was made before the aircraft was fully under control. Nothing further was flown by IP.
texts.2: SP, due to a momentary reaction to the other aircraft's abort, reduced power briefly before recognizing that neither an element abort had been directed nor any malfunction existed. SP advanced the PCL to MAX, held the respective side of the runway and completed a normal single ship takeoff, making the radio call only once the aircraft was under control.
texts.3: SP recognized that the other aircraft's abort was not an element abort, advanced the PCL to MAX power, maintained his respective side of the runway and executed a normal single ship takeoff. Aircraft control was never sacrificed to make the radio call, which followed as soon as practical. Engine instruments and airspeed were crosschecked before the decision was made.
texts.4: SP crosschecked engine instruments and airspeed, established that no element abort had been directed and continued the takeoff with the PCL at MAX, holding his respective side of the runway throughout the roll and the separation. The radio call was made only after control was assured, and the rejoin was flown after becoming safely airborne. Departures from the published abort and continued takeoff technique were negligible.
texts.marginal: SP continued the takeoff correctly and stayed on his respective side of the runway, but a brief power reduction accompanied the other aircraft's call before the decision was made. The crosscheck of engine instruments and airspeed was completed and the radio call was correctly deferred. SP is expected to hold the power setting while the crosscheck is made, since a sympathetic reaction adds a second aircraft to a high speed abort.

texts_at.1: SP advanced the PCL to MAX and completed a normal single ship takeoff, though power had been reduced and the abort begun before SP had to be told to continue, with power restored late in the available runway and the radio call made before the aircraft was fully under control. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training. SP is expected to crosscheck engine instruments and airspeed before reacting to the other aircraft's call, before the verbal prompt on the next sortie.
texts_at.2: SP briefly reduced power after a momentary reaction to the other aircraft's abort, recognizing that neither an element abort had been directed nor any malfunction existed, advancing the PCL to MAX, holding the respective side of the runway and completing a normal single ship takeoff, with the radio call made only once the aircraft was under control. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to crosscheck engine instruments and airspeed before reducing power so the momentary reaction does not occur.
texts_at.3: SP continued the takeoff correctly and stayed on the respective side of the runway within standards, though a brief power reduction accompanied the other aircraft's call before the decision was made, with the crosscheck of engine instruments and airspeed completed and the radio call correctly deferred. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to hold the power setting while the crosscheck is made, since a sympathetic reaction adds a second aircraft to a high speed abort.

texts_above.2: SP briefly reduced power after a momentary reaction to the other aircraft's abort, recognizing that neither an element abort had been directed nor any malfunction existed, advancing the PCL to MAX, holding the respective side of the runway and completing a normal single ship takeoff, with no prompting from the IP and the radio call made only once the aircraft was under control. Crosschecking engine instruments and airspeed before reducing power would remove the momentary reaction entirely. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to sound recovery of the power setting once the crosscheck was made.
texts_above.3: SP recognized that the other aircraft's abort was not an element abort, advanced the PCL to MAX power, maintained the respective side of the runway and executed a normal single ship takeoff, with aircraft control never sacrificed to make the radio call, which followed as soon as practical, and engine instruments and airspeed crosschecked before the decision was made. The only refinement left is to hold the same crosscheck discipline on an abort call heard later in the roll. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to sure-handed crosscheck discipline before reacting to the other aircraft's call.
texts_above.4: SP crosschecked engine instruments and airspeed, established that no element abort had been directed and continued the takeoff with the PCL at MAX, holding the respective side of the runway throughout the roll and the separation, with the radio call made only after control was assured and the rejoin flown after becoming safely airborne, with deviations from the published abort and continued takeoff technique negligible. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exceptional crosscheck discipline that kept the takeoff continuing without a sympathetic reaction.

error_modes.label: Evasive maneuvering for a bird and responsibilities after a midair between members
error_modes.source: technique:9.44-9.47 ENGINE PROBLEMS, PHYSIOLOGICAL INCIDENT, BIRD STRIKE, MIDAIR COLLISION

texts.0: SP, startled by the bird appearing in the windscreen, maneuvered abruptly toward the other aircraft's flight path in an attempt to avoid it, so that avoiding a midair collision was never treated as the primary concern. Separation was not ensured before the condition of the aircraft was assessed and the recovery plan was built without it. IP took the aircraft to restore the separation.
texts.1: SP, due to the reaction to the bird being made without reference to the other aircraft's position, began the avoidance in the direction of the formation and reversed it only when directed. Separation was restored at the limit of what remained acceptable and the sequence of ensuring separation before handling the strike was carried out step by step on verbal direction.
texts.2: SP, due to a first input made toward the formation, briefly reduced the separation before recognizing the other aircraft's position and reversing the maneuver unaided. Separation was ensured before the aircraft condition was assessed, the strike was reported and the restricted forward visibility was accounted for in the recovery plan. No IP input was required.
texts.3: SP maneuvered away from the other aircraft's position rather than into it, ensured separation before handling the strike, and then assessed damage, controllability and forward visibility with the other member's assistance. The recovery plan accounted for the restricted forward visibility, including the option of a crab landing, and SP stated that after a collision between formation members they shall not act as chase ships for each other.
texts.4: SP kept avoidance of a midair collision and aircraft separation as the primary concern throughout, maneuvering clear of the formation and confirming separation before any other action. The damage assessment, the recovery plan with the crab landing option for restricted forward visibility, and the requirement for separate clearances and independent chase ships after a collision between members were all stated without prompting. Deviations from the published guidance were negligible.
texts.marginal: SP avoided the bird clear of the other aircraft and stayed within standards, but the first input was made before the other aircraft's position had been reconfirmed, and separation was verified only afterwards. The subsequent assessment and recovery plan were sound. SP is expected to fix the other aircraft's position as the reference for any avoidance input, since the primary concern is avoiding the midair rather than avoiding the bird.

texts_at.1: SP reversed the avoidance manoeuvre and restored separation, though the reversal followed only once directed and the avoidance had begun in the direction of the formation, with separation restored at the limit of what remained acceptable and the sequence of ensuring separation before handling the strike carried out step by step on verbal direction. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training. SP is expected to reference the other aircraft's position before the first avoidance input, before the verbal prompt on the next sortie.
texts_at.2: SP briefly reduced separation with a first input made toward the formation, recognizing the other aircraft's position and reversing the manoeuvre unaided, so separation was ensured before the aircraft condition was assessed, the strike was reported and the restricted forward visibility was accounted for in the recovery plan, with no IP input required. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to reference the other aircraft's position before the first input so the reduction in separation is avoided.
texts_at.3: SP avoided the bird clear of the other aircraft and stayed within standards, though the first input was made before the other aircraft's position had been reconfirmed, with separation verified only afterwards, and the subsequent assessment and recovery plan sound. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to fix the other aircraft's position as the reference for any avoidance input, since the primary concern is avoiding the midair rather than avoiding the bird.

texts_above.2: SP briefly reduced separation with a first input made toward the formation, recognizing the other aircraft's position and reversing the manoeuvre unaided, so separation was ensured before the aircraft condition was assessed, the strike was reported and the restricted forward visibility was accounted for in the recovery plan, with no prompting from the IP. Referencing the other aircraft's position before the first input would remove the reduction in separation entirely. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to solid recovery of separation once the other aircraft's position was referenced.
texts_above.3: SP maneuvered away from the other aircraft's position rather than into it, ensured separation before handling the strike, and then assessed damage, controllability and forward visibility with the other member's assistance, with the recovery plan accounting for the restricted forward visibility, including the option of a crab landing, and SP stated that after a collision between formation members they shall not act as chase ships for each other. The only refinement left is to hold the same reference to the other aircraft's position when startled by a second, unrelated event. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to well-developed discipline in referencing the other aircraft's position before reacting.
texts_above.4: SP kept avoidance of a midair collision and aircraft separation as the primary concern throughout, maneuvering clear of the formation and confirming separation before any other action, with the damage assessment, the recovery plan with the crab landing option for restricted forward visibility, and the requirement for separate clearances and independent chase ships after a collision between members all stated without prompting, and deviations from the published guidance negligible. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to outstanding discipline that kept separation the primary concern before any other action.
